researchUpdates.title: Fabrication of a three-dimensional superhydrophobic alkali-activated geopolymer material and its epoxy composite coating via sol-gel synergistic modification
researchUpdates.authors: Tenglong Li, Jinliang Song, Wanshu Liu, Hongli Xu, Annan Jiang and Guoping Zhang
researchUpdates.summary: A sol–gel route combines two silane modifiers with an alkali-activated geopolymer powder, then incorporates that powder into an epoxy mortar to test whether water repellency extends through the coating rather than remaining only at its surface.
highlights: The study treats hydrophobicity as a bulk composite design problem and evaluates it alongside adhesion, abrasion, chemical exposure, water uptake and icing-related tests.

Reported coating durability belongs to the tested geopolymer powder, silane chemistry, epoxy matrix and laboratory exposure protocols; it does not by itself demonstrate service life on full-scale concrete structures.
researchUpdates.access: Publisher-indexed metadata and abstract-level evidence were reviewed; the full methods and underlying data were not independently audited. The work concerns a geopolymer-derived additive in an epoxy composite coating, not a structural geopolymer concrete. Contact angle, adhesion, abrasion, chemical stability, icing delay and water absorption are distinct outcomes and are not converted into unreported compressive, tensile, shear or flexural strength.
researchUpdates.summaryBasis: Primary Elsevier publisher metadata and indexed abstract-level evidence; no abstract text, publisher highlights, figures, tables or full-paper passages were reproduced

researchUpdates.title: Freeze–thaw performance of ambient-cured geopolymer concrete: An integrated mechanical, bond, and microstructural comparison with C50/60 normal concrete
researchUpdates.authors: Mahmud Yağan, Zinnur Çelik and Fatih Mehmet Özkal
researchUpdates.summary: An ambient-cured geopolymer concrete and a C50/60 conventional concrete are followed through as many as 300 freeze–thaw cycles using separate compression, flexure, splitting tension, reinforcement-bond, mass, ultrasonic and microstructural measurements.
highlights: The tested geopolymer began near the control concrete in compressive strength but deteriorated sharply after prolonged cycling, so high initial strength should not be used as a proxy for freeze–thaw resilience.
Bond retention, compression, flexure and splitting tension are reported as separate responses; the severe bond loss cannot be relabeled as shear or assumed to predict the other mechanical tests.
researchUpdates.access: Publisher-indexed metadata and abstract-level evidence were reviewed; direct full-paper methods, raw data and statistical details were not independently audited. This is one formulation compared with one conventional concrete under a specified accelerated cycling protocol. The results are not an independent replication of all ambient-cured geopolymer concretes and do not establish field service life.
researchUpdates.summaryBasis: Primary Elsevier publisher metadata and indexed abstract-level evidence; no abstract text, publisher highlights, figures, tables or full-paper passages were reproduced

journalArticle.title: Durability needs the right response variable
journalArticle.summary: Two new studies show why a durable-material claim must name both the exposure and the measured response.
paragraphs: The coating study examines wetting, adhesion, abrasion, chemical exposure and icing behavior, while the concrete study separates freeze–thaw changes in compression, flexure, splitting tension and reinforcement bond. Neither can be compressed into a single universal durability score without discarding important evidence.

For cataloging, keep the exposure protocol, specimen and substrate, cycle count or duration, conditioning history and each response variable together. A favorable surface or transport result is not a strength result, and acceptable initial compression does not establish retained bond or freeze–thaw performance.
